headline.en: The crash happened in code from {owner:m}, near the top of the call stack.

why_not_sure.en: Code near the top of the stack is often where a crash shows, not where it started.

headline.en: Code from {owner:m} was on the call stack when the game crashed.
The game was handling a record from {owner:p} when it crashed.

why_not_sure.en: A record in use when the game crashed may be a victim rather than the cause.

headline.en: A record from {owner:p} was nearby in memory when the game crashed.
The game was handling the file {owner:f} when it crashed.

why_not_sure.en: A damaged file is a common cause, but this one may only have been in use.

text.en: The game ran out of memory, which can make any code crash, so a mod named here may only be where it ran out.

headline.en: The game ran out of memory. A larger Windows page file, or fewer high-resolution textures, often helps.

why_not_sure.en: A mod can cause the memory use, but the log does not say which.

headline.en: A DLL could not load another library it needs. A missing requirement, or a mod built for a different game version, is a common reason.

why_not_sure.en: The log does not say which library was missing.

headline.en: The game stopped while reading its installed-content catalog, on a value it expected to be a number. Another game build on this PC can rewrite ContentCatalog.txt in a format this build cannot read; moving that file aside lets the game rebuild it.

why_not_sure.en: This names the file the game was reading, not the mod or tool that changed it.

headline.en: This crash sits at an engine location that load orders with missing masters or unsupported ESL-format plugins reach. Check the missing-master list, and whether backported ESL support is needed for this game build.

why_not_sure.en: The location says the load order was incomplete; it does not name which plugin was missing.

headline.en: The crash was a divide-by-zero, and Climates of Tamriel is loaded. This mod is known to reach that failure through one of its records; replacing it or clearing the affected record from the save is the usual next step.

why_not_sure.en: A loaded mod that has had this failure reported is a lead, not a proof.

headline.en: The fault is inside d3d11.dll, where a graphics injector such as ENB or ReShade puts its code. An injector binary built for a different game build is one common reason.

why_not_sure.en: The log does not say which injector, if any, is installed.

headline.en: The crash reached KERNELBASE.dll with the Skyrim Upscaler on the stack. This pairing has been reported on Windows 11 24H2 with DLAA; disabling the upscaler is a small test.

why_not_sure.en: The log does not state the Windows build, so the 24H2 link is a report, not a check.

headline.en: The Dragon's Eye Minimap plugin is loaded and camera or image-space objects are on the stack. Toggling the minimap off is a quick test before a longer investigation.

why_not_sure.en: The plugin is one of several things that can produce this stack shape.

headline.en: SkyClimb is older than the release its author lists as compatible with this game build. Updating it, or using the build for this game version, is a small first step.

why_not_sure.en: An old SkyClimb on a newer game is a known cause of crashes, but this log does not show that it was the one that crashed.

headline.en: A hair mesh ({hair}) was being handled when the game crashed. Hair mods, and the physics mods that move hair, are a common cause of crashes like this: check that each is up to date and made for this game version.

why_not_sure.en: Hair is everywhere on screen, so it may only have been in use.

headline.en: A hair mesh ({hair}) was being handled when the game crashed, and HDT-SMP physics is installed. SMP hair on NPCs is a known source of random crashes: make sure HDT-SMP and your hair mods are current, and consider the SMP-NPC crash fix mod.

why_not_sure.en: Hair is everywhere on screen, so it may only have been in use.

text.en: SSE Engine Fixes is older than 7.0.20. Newer versions prevent some crash types, so updating it is a cheap step (carry over any settings you changed in its .toml file).

headline.en: SSE Engine Fixes could be updated.
The game crashed while drawing shadows, and this Engine Fixes version is older than 7.0.18, which fixes a crash of this kind. Updating SSE Engine Fixes is the first thing to try.

why_not_sure.en: Shadow drawing is involved in many crashes; the update fixes one known kind.

text.en: This log comes from an older Crash Logger. Version 1.20.1 or later writes more detail, which makes the next crash easier to diagnose.

headline.en: Crash Logger could be updated.

{owner:d} is listed as a script-extender plugin, and its file declares it was built for a game version other than the one that crashed. Updating it, or using the build made for this game version, is the first thing to try.

why_not_sure.en: A DLL built for another game version is a known cause of crashes, but the log cannot show that this DLL was the one that failed.

headline.en: The exception line names {owner:d} as the module that faulted. That is the crash site; it can be where a fault shows rather than where it started.

why_not_sure.en: Being at the fault address shows where the game stopped, not who set the failure up.

headline.en: The fault is inside {shader_module}, where ENB, ReShade or DXVK puts its own copy. An injector binary built for a different game version, or a mismatched preset, is a common reason; the graphics driver is the other. The log cannot say which copy was loaded.

why_not_sure.en: The log sees the DLL's name, not the folder it was loaded from.

headline.en: SKSE refused to load {owner:d} because it is built for a different game version. It could not be running in this session, so it is not the code that crashed, but the mismatch is a real problem to fix: update it, or use the build made for this game version.

why_not_sure.en: This names a plugin the game did not load; the crash itself may have another cause.

headline.en: SKSE refused to load {owner:d} because the Address Library for this game version is missing or out of date. Installing the Address Library build for this game version, or the plugin build made for it, is the usual fix. The plugin never ran in this session.

why_not_sure.en: This names a plugin the game did not load; the crash itself may have another cause.

headline.en: SKSE refused to load {owner:d} because it needs a newer SKSE than the one installed. Updating SKSE to the build for this game version is the usual fix. The plugin never ran in this session.

why_not_sure.en: This names a plugin the game did not load; the crash itself may have another cause.

headline.en: SKSE refused to load {owner:d} because its version data is invalid, or it is not an SKSE plugin at all. Reinstalling the build made for this game version is the usual fix. The plugin never ran in this session.

why_not_sure.en: This names a plugin the game did not load; the crash itself may have another cause.

headline.en: SKSE refused to load {owner:d}: it is a 32-bit plugin from the older game, which this 64-bit game cannot load. Use the Special Edition build of it, or remove it.

why_not_sure.en: This names a plugin the game did not load; the crash itself may have another cause.

headline.en: SKSE could not load {owner:d} because another DLL it needs is missing (error 126). Installing the missing requirement, or a complete build of this plugin, is the usual fix.

why_not_sure.en: The log names the plugin that failed, not the missing library itself.

headline.en: SKSE reported that {owner:d} did not finish loading. Reinstalling the build made for this game version, or removing it, is the usual fix. Removing a plugin partway through a playthrough can damage a save, so back up the save or test on a new game first.

why_not_sure.en: The log says this plugin failed to load; it does not prove the failure caused the crash.

text.en: A crash suppressor is loaded, so the log may not describe the real failure. Test again with it disabled before trusting any name here.
SkyrimCrashGuard is a crash suppressor: it can hide the original fault, so this evidence is weaker than usual.

headline.en: A crash suppressor is loaded.

text.en: This location is where an externally closed process often stops, so the log may be incomplete.
If you or a tool closed the game, this is not a crash.

headline.en: The game stopped at a location where a process closed from outside often stops.

The crash was an in-page error: Windows could not read a page of a file the game was using. A file that moved or is unreadable, a disk problem, or an antivirus lock can cause it. Checking the drive and the game's files is a sensible first step.

why_not_sure.en: The log names the mechanism, not the file that could not be read.

headline.en: The crash was a stack overflow, usually runaway recursion: a script, a mod, or a save with a cyclic structure is the common source. It is a different failure from a plain access violation.

why_not_sure.en: The log names the mechanism, not the code that recursed.

headline.en: Windows reported heap corruption. The heap was already damaged before this point, so the crash site cannot name the corrupter; testing recent changes one at a time is the reliable way to find it.

why_not_sure.en: The code that noticed the damage is rarely the code that caused it.

headline.en: The graphics device was lost: the message names a DXGI device-removed or device-hung failure. The graphics driver, an overclock, heat or power are the usual reasons, not a mod. Updating or rolling back the driver is a small first test.

why_not_sure.en: The log names the device failure, not what made the driver give up.

headline.en: The game stopped on a breakpoint or assertion, which a mod's own check can raise. The first non-system module on the stack is the usual place to start looking.

why_not_sure.en: An assertion says a check failed; it does not say which mod set it off.

headline.en: The fault is inside dxgi.dll. A graphics injector such as ReShade or DXVK often puts its own dxgi.dll in the game folder, and a build for a different game version is a common reason; the graphics driver is the other. The log cannot say which dxgi.dll was loaded.

why_not_sure.en: The log sees the DLL's name, not the folder it was loaded from.

headline.en: The fault is inside dinput8.dll, where an input mod or an overlay puts its own copy. The log cannot say whether the Windows copy or a game-folder copy was loaded; checking the mods that install dinput8.dll is the sensible first step.

why_not_sure.en: The log sees the DLL's name, not the folder it was loaded from.

headline.en: The crash is inside the game's save code. That names the subsystem, not a mod: a save, a missing master or a setting can all reach it. Removing mods partway through a playthrough can damage a save, so back up the save or test on a new game first.

why_not_sure.en: Crashing while saving does not show that the save itself is damaged.

headline.en: The crash is inside the game's save-loading code. That names the subsystem, not a mod: a save, a missing master or a recently changed asset can all reach it. Test a new game or a backup of the save before changing the load order, because removing mods partway through a playthrough can damage a save.

why_not_sure.en: Crashing while loading does not show that the save itself is damaged.

rules.reference: Phostwood js/diagnoses.js:1763 (GPL-3, idea); names from crash/addrlib-names.json

headline.en: A record the game was using is marked deleted. A mod or the save removed a record that something still points at. Removing mods partway through a playthrough can damage a save, so back up the save or test on a new game first.

why_not_sure.en: The deleted record's owner is not necessarily the mod that deleted it.

headline.en: A record's object reference is None: it points at an object that is not there. A missing master, a deleted record or a save that no longer matches the load order can leave this behind. Back up the save and check the missing-master list first.

why_not_sure.en: The log shows the empty reference, not which plugin removed the object.

text.en: An object in memory has a form id in the FF range, which the save generates at run time. It belongs to the save rather than a mod's static record, so it is not by itself evidence against the plugin that appears with it.

headline.en: A run-time object from the save was in memory.

The crash log lists only {total} plugins, fewer than a working game loads, so the load order may not have finished loading. Check the missing-master list and whether a plugin stops the game while it reads the plugin list.

why_not_sure.en: A short list shows the load order was incomplete; it does not say why.
